How Renewable Energy Is Blowing Climate Change Efforts Off Course

A pretty goofy article since it's dooming and glooming over something with an incredibly obvious solution.

  • Problem: The electricity production from renewables comes in huge bursts followed by periods of minimal production.
  • Solution: There's this fancy thing that allows you to store electricity for later use: a battery. Coincidentally Elon Musk is behind the construction of what will be the second largest building in the world. What is that building used for? Manufacturing batteries.

I suspect the energy industry is lobbying to make the future nuclear instead of solar. It has nothing to do with the viability of either method, but the profitability. Nuclear is centralized and has enormous barriers to entry. Costs will be regulated but in general the population will be forced to pay whatever the government decides a 'fair fee' is. Solar by contrast allows people to take energy production into their own hands. These batteries, in many areas, mean you don't even need the central grid. Set up your own cells and batteries and you'll be able to live while paying exactly $0 for electricity. And those cells and batteries last on the order of decades. That is a radical shift away from our current situation where we spend literally trillions of dollars on energy.

To me it's the issue of commercial versus consumer use. While renewable energy shows promise for meeting consumer needs, the number of new plants needed to drag the rest of the world into the industrial age will need other energy production methods, nuclear fission being the current best and viable option. That will shift to fusion hopefully over the next 100 years but currently there is only fission.

Google is one of the largest companies in the world. Today more than 35% of their operations are currently powered by renewables. And that's in a world where progress in the transition towards renewables has been hamstrung by economics meaning their options are limited.

I'm for renewable energy as much as the next person, but I'm also pragmatic enough to realize that it can't solve the world's current energy needs. We need nuclear power in addition to renewables+batteries, ideally with the nuclear plants replacing the current fossil fuel plants and then individuals subsidizing their power needs with solar panels.

If for some reason the supervolcano under Yellowstone National Park were to go off tomorrow, the entire world would be plunged into a miniature ice age by the ashes from the eruption. All solar panels would be rendered next to useless. A lot of wind farms would also be screwed because of ash buildup in their mechanical bits. Nuclear fission/fusion plants would be nearly unaffected, though, and produce far more energy than either renewables or fossil fuels.

Another problem I have with the "use batteries" solution is that creating batteries has a very real environmental impact, from mining the metals to create them to transporting said metals halfway around the world to actually build them, to shipping them halfway back around the world to actually sell them.

The nice thing about solar is that the energy is, relative to our needs, effectively infinite. Right now more harvestable energy hits the Earth's surface in 2 hours1 than the entire earth uses in a year. The limiting factor is not in the availability of the energy, but in simply constructing the devices to harness it. Build the devices and the energy is there. If you'd rather go more creative than brute force there is infinite room for technical innovation and creativity in the field. For instance China and Japan are now actively researching and developing space based solar power systems. They harvest the energy in space at max efficiency in exchange for transmitting it back to earth. In 2015 Japan performed a successful proof of concept. Solar energy is a field that hasn't had its potential even begin to be tapped. As our species grows and expands it will almost certainly be the primary power source. Not only does it have the greatest potential but it's also the safest.

Yes, it has great potential, but the technology isn't there yet. Nuclear fission, however, already has the technology and can produce far more power than renewables or fossil fuels with a small carbon footprint. It's also only further proof that nuclear fusion is a far better energy source than anything else, as that's what powers the sun.

As for your source, allow me to quote from page 10 (I inserted the dagger footnote marker):

This theoretical potential could be used to generate 15 TW of C-neutral power from 10%-efficient† solar-conversion systems covering only 0.17% of the earth's surface area, or [...] 858,792 km2. This area is roughly the land area of Namibia (825,418 km2) or Venezuela (882,050 km2).

To supply the (smaller) power that the U.S. consumed in 2001 (3.24 TW) with similarly efficient solar conversion systems would require a correspondingly smaller surface area, [...] 185,500 km2. This is roughly 1.9% of the surface area (9,361,418 km2), and 2.0% of the land area (9,161,923 km2), of the U.S. (CIA 2005). It is also roughly 30 times the total roof space (5,800 km2) that was estimated to be available in 2003 for photovoltaics in the U.S. It is comparable to the 1-1.5% of the U.S. land area that is covered by the nation's public roads; and is comparable to the land area of North Dakota (178,694 km2) or South Dakota (196,576 km2).

† Most solar panels in 2016 have a peak efficiency of 11-15%, but consumer solar panels (the vast majority of solar panels) average less than that because they tend to be fixed-angle, which reduces the amount of time they spend at ideal angles to the sun.

Ignoring the fact that the world's energy needs have almost certainly increased in the decade since this PDF was published in 2006, thereby increasing the area of land that would need to be covered by solar panels, these are absolutely humongous swathes of land that you're talking about covering with solar panels. In order to do this, we're talking about demolishing entire forests, fields of arable farmland, etc. in order to put down solar panels, because there isn't nearly enough roof space in the world for all of them (as pointed out by the sentence I formatted in oblique text). There would also be a large public push against putting solar panels all over the place, even if they were in relatively uninhabited places like deserts, because they harm the natural ecology of the land.

To this rational (in my mind, at least) argument, you may respond, "Replace the roads with solar panels! Other countries are trying it!" This introduces all sorts of potential infrastructure issues, though, and still doesn't address the fact that even according to the PDF, only 1.5% of the 2% or more of the United State's surface area that would be required for the U.S. alone is covered by roads. Other countries don't have as extensive of a road network as the U.S. has, and would therefore have an even larger surface area deficit when transitioning to solar power.

Even the "space based solar power systems" that you say Japan and China are developing, if they are completed, would have massive problems, from maintenance to impacts on ecology underneath them. We would still need an array of some sort to capture the energy on the ground, and then we would need to maintain the fleet of hundreds if not thousands of geosynchronous satellites necessary to redirect the sun's energy to Earth. Oh, and...

They harvest the energy in space at max efficiency in exchange for transmitting it back to earth.

...at ~50% efficiency. This combined with the fact that they still wouldn't be able to beam the energy through clouds, production costs would be gigantic, and we're talking about putting massive lasers or microwave transmitters which might be weaponized in space makes them a terrible proposition for solving the energy problem.

Nuclear power, on the other hand, requires a fraction of the land footprint that our current fossil fuel plants require right now due to their increased power output and can only be locally weaponized instead of pointed anywhere on the planet. Despite cries of "But the nuclear waste!" from most environmentalists, if we built breeder reactors, the vast majority of the nuclear waste would be relatively safe nuclear byproducts that would not need to be stored for billions of years like the byproducts of current American reactors, which are currently forbidden by law from being breeder reactors. They're also far safer than any of our fossil fuel plants, and nuclear fusion reactors would have the potential to outlast humanity just like the sun, given enough fuel.
